questions.stem: Fundamental Duties were incorporated in the Indian Constitution by which amendment?
questions.explanation: 42nd Amendment (1976) added Part IV-A (Article 51A) with 10 Fundamental Duties on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee. The 86th Amendment (2002) added the 11th duty (education for children).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are enshrined in which Part of the Indian Constitution?
questions.explanation: DPSPs: Part IV (Articles 36-51). Fundamental Rights: Part III. Fundamental Duties: Part IV-A.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: DPSPs are inspired by which country's constitution?
questions.explanation: DPSPs were borrowed from the Irish Constitution (Bunreacht na hEireann, 1937), which itself drew from the Spanish Republican Constitution of 1931.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to secure equal pay for equal work for both men and women?
questions.explanation: Article 39(d): The State shall direct its policy towards securing equal pay for equal work for both men and women. This is a DPSP.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 'Uniform Civil Code' is directed by which Article?
questions.explanation: Article 44 DPSP: The State shall endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code for the citizens throughout the territory of India.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which Fundamental Duty was added by the 86th Constitutional Amendment?

options.option_text: A parent/guardian to provide opportunity for education to children aged 6-14
To protect and improve the natural environment
To uphold and protect sovereignty of India

questions.explanation: 86th Amendment (2002) added the 11th Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k): to provide educational opportunity for children between 6-14 years (linked to the Right to Education Act).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: In the landmark Minerva Mills case (1980), the Supreme Court held that:

options.option_text: Parliament cannot destroy the Fundamental Rights while implementing DPSPs — balance must be maintained
DPSPs are superior to Fundamental Rights
DPSPs can be enforced in courts

questions.explanation: Minerva Mills (1980): the Court struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that had given primacy to DPSPs over Fundamental Rights. Held that harmony between Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which category of DPSPs is classified as 'Gandhian principles'?

options.option_text: Organisation of village panchayats, prohibition of intoxicants, cottage industries promotion

questions.explanation: Gandhian DPSPs (Articles 40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48) include: village panchayats (Art. 40), cottage industries (Art. 43), prohibition (Art. 47), animal husbandry (Art. 48), etc.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Article 51 of the DPSP directs India to:

options.option_text: Promote international peace and security and respect for international law
Establish free legal aid for the poor

questions.explanation: Article 51 (International Peace): State to promote international peace, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Are Directive Principles of State Policy justiciable (enforceable in courts)?

options.option_text: No — they are non-justiciable but fundamental in governance
Yes — courts can strike down laws violating them
Yes — but only at the Supreme Court level
It depends on the specific Article

questions.explanation: DPSPs are non-justiciable (Article 37: 'shall not be enforceable by any court'). However, they are fundamental in governance and courts use them to interpret laws and review legislation.
